title: Secrets in Git, Safely: SOPS and Sealed Secrets
intro: GitOps wants everything in Git, and a secret in Git in plain text is a leak. Two tools solve it by committing only encrypted values: SOPS encrypts the values inside a YAML file, and Sealed Secrets encrypts a whole Kubernetes Secret so that only the cluster can open it. You're in a repository with a plain file, secrets.yaml, that must not be committed as it is.

steps.prompt: Encrypt secrets.yaml in place with SOPS. (The repository's .sops.yaml already says which keys to encrypt for.)
steps.fake_output:
(no output: secrets.yaml rewritten)

$ cat secrets.yaml
db_password: ENC[AES256_GCM,data:9cJx2vA=,iv:...,tag:...,type:str]
api_key: ENC[AES256_GCM,data:Tz81Lw4hQ==,iv:...,tag:...,type:str]
sops:
    age:
        - recipient: age1examplerecipientpublickey0000000000000000000000000000000
    lastmodified: "2026-09-28T11:50:00Z"
steps.explanation: The keys are still readable; every value is encrypted. A 'sops' block records who can decrypt.
steps.why: Encrypting values but not keys is SOPS's best feature: a diff in a pull request still shows which secret changed, without showing what it is. The file's data key is itself encrypted for each recipient: age or PGP keys, or better, a cloud KMS key, so that access is controlled by IAM and nobody has a key file to lose.

steps.prompt: Check you can still read it: decrypt secrets.yaml to the terminal.
steps.explanation: Decrypted to the terminal only; the file on disk stays encrypted.
steps.why: Plain 'sops secrets.yaml' opens the decrypted content in your editor and re-encrypts on save, so plain text never needs to exist as a file. Argo CD and Flux can decrypt SOPS files at deploy time, with the cluster holding the key. Don't redirect the decrypted output into a file inside the repository.

steps.prompt: A new team member's key has been added to .sops.yaml. Re-encrypt the file's data key so the new list of recipients can open it.
steps.fake_output:
2026/09/28 11:52:14 Syncing keys for file secrets.yaml
The following changes will be made to the file's groups:
+++ age1examplenewmemberpublickey00000000000000000000000000000000
Is this okay? (y/n): y
2026/09/28 11:52:16 File secrets.yaml synced with new keys
steps.explanation: The new recipient can now decrypt, and the secret values themselves were not re-encrypted.
steps.why: Adding a reader is cheap. Removing one is not: someone who could decrypt yesterday may have a copy, and the old ciphertext is still in Git history. So when a person leaves, updating the recipients isn't enough; the secrets themselves must be rotated at the source. That's true of every scheme that puts encrypted secrets in Git.

steps.prompt: The other approach. You have an ordinary Kubernetes Secret manifest, secret.yaml. Turn it into a SealedSecret in YAML, written to sealedsecret.yaml.
steps.fake_output:
(no output: sealedsecret.yaml written)

apiVersion: bitnami.com/v1alpha1
kind: SealedSecret
metadata:
  name: shop-db
  namespace: shop
spec:
  encryptedData:
    password: AgBy3i4OJSWK+PiTySYZZA9rO43cGDEq...
steps.explanation: A SealedSecret that's safe to commit. Only the controller in the cluster can turn it back into a Secret.
steps.why: kubeseal encrypts with the cluster controller's public key, so anyone can seal and nobody but the cluster can unseal: developers can add secrets without being able to read existing ones. The sealed value is bound to its name and namespace, so it can't be copied into another namespace to be read there. Delete secret.yaml afterwards, and make sure it's in .gitignore.

steps.prompt:
What must you back up for Sealed Secrets to survive losing the cluster?
  a) Nothing: the SealedSecrets are in Git
  b) The controller's private sealing keys, because without them every SealedSecret in Git is undecryptable
  c) The kubeseal binary
  d) The plain secret.yaml files
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
$ kubectl get secret -n kube-system -l sealedsecrets.bitnami.com/sealed-secrets-key
NAME                      TYPE                DATA   AGE
sealed-secrets-keyx7m2q   kubernetes.io/tls   2      120d
steps.hint: The files in Git are encrypted. Where is the key that opens them?
steps.explanation: The private keys live only in the cluster. Lose it without a backup and the secrets are gone.
steps.why: This is the trade-off against SOPS with a cloud KMS key, where the key outlives any cluster. Store a copy of the sealing keys somewhere safe (a secrets manager, not Git), and test restoring them into a fresh cluster. The controller generates a new key every 30 days and keeps the old ones, so back up all of them.
